newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Asia chipmakers shrug off EU anti-dumping move.
newsitem.headline: Asia chipmakers shrug off EU anti-dumping move.

text.p: Chipmakers from Japan and South Korea on Tuesday shrugged off the European Union's decision to impose anti-dumping duties on their microchip exports, while their competitors in Taiwan cheered the move.

All the major producers in Asia, including Singapore, said EU's decision to reintroduce minimum prices for DRAM computer chips from South Korea and Japan on April 1 would not adversely affect their businesses.
"We think that the move would not have a major impact on our chip business," a spokeswoman for Japanese chipmaker Fujitsu Ltd said.

"I think it is quite specific to Japan and Korea. We are not aware that this is going to be levied on ASEAN (the Association of Southeast Asian Nations)," said William Liu, chairman of SFCI, a private industry group in Singapore.
Liu said the EU's move, which targets 12 Japanese and three Korean companies, would not have an immediate impact on DRAM chip producers in the region.

Share prices fell on Tuesday for South Korea's three memory chip makers -- Samsung Electronics, LG Semicon and Hyundai Electronics. However, analysts attributed the declines to overall market weakness rather than to tighter EU policy.
"I don't see any direct impact (from the EU's move) on the three firms' share prices. The falls were due to the gloomy mood on the overall market," said Lee Gyu-bum, an analyst at Hyundai Securities.

Taiwan firms welcomed the EU's decision, saying the imposition of an anti-dumping tax was inevitable in the face of stiff competition from Japan and South Korea whose products outperform European offerings.
"It's more bullish than bearish to us because it will help boost our competitiveness," said Ruth Pao, spokeswoman for TI-Acer, a subsidiary of Taiwan's computer giant Acer Inc.
Pao said she expected the tax, which EU officials have declined to specify, to be high to protect European makers.
But other firms on the island warned of harmful effects of such a tax, calling it a protectionist practice that in the long run may hurt Taiwan.
European officials said the measure would take effect on April 1 and duties will be introduced gradually to avoid harming the EU chip market, where DRAM prices have been low.
The EU market for DRAM chips was worth five billion European currency units (US$5.7 billion) in 1995.
The EU first imposed anti-dumping duties on Japanese exporters in January 1990 and later on Korean exporters. The measures were suspended 21 months ago due to a rise in DRAM prices.
DRAM prices tumbled on the world market in 1996 due to oversupply.
